title: Λύκοι καὶ πρόβατα καὶ κριός
titleEn: The Wolves, the Sheep and the Ram
part: The Wolves, the Sheep and the Ram (Chambry 218)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 218. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Λύκοι πρέσβεις ἔστειλαν τοῖς προβάτοις εἰρήνην ποιῆσαι μετ’ αὐτῶν διηνεκῆ, εἰ τοὺς κύνας λάβωσι καὶ διαφθείρωσι.
sentences.tr: Lykoi presbeis esteilan tois probatois eirēnēn poiēsai met’ autōn diēnekē, ei tous kynas labōsi kai diaphtheirōsi.
sentences.l: Wolves sent envoys to the sheep, to make an unbroken peace with them, if they should get the dogs and destroy them.
sentences.n: ποιῆσαι is an infinitive of purpose after a verb of sending: they were sent in order to make peace. διηνεκής is 'running right through', of a peace with no break in it. The subject of λάβωσι and διαφθείρωσι is the wolves — the dogs are what they are to be given. εἰ with the subjunctive and no ἄν is not the strict Attic form — one would expect ἐάν — but the sense is the ordinary vivid future condition.

sentences.t: Τὰ μωρὰ δὲ πρόβατα συνέθεντο τοῦτο ποιῆσαι.
sentences.tr: Ta mōra de probata synethento touto poiēsai.
sentences.l: And the foolish sheep agreed to do this.
sentences.n: συντίθεμαι in the middle is to put terms together for oneself, hence to come to an agreement. Chambry's narrator calls the sheep μωρά outright, before the ram has said a word.

sentences.t: Ἀλλά τις γέρων κριὸς εἶπεν· « Πῶς ὑμῖν πιστεύσω καὶ συνοικήσω, ὅπου, καὶ τῶν κυνῶν φυλαττόντων με, ἀκινδύνως νέμεσθαι οὐ δυνατόν μοι ; »
sentences.tr: Alla tis gerōn krios eipen· « Pōs hymin pisteusō kai synoikēsō, hopou, kai tōn kynōn phylattontōn me, akindynōs nemesthai ou dynaton moi ; »
sentences.l: But a certain old ram said: « How shall I trust you and live-together-with you, when, even with the dogs guarding me, it is not possible for me to graze without danger? »
sentences.i: But an old ram said: « How am I to trust you and share a life with you, when even with the dogs on guard over me I cannot graze in safety? »
sentences.n: πιστεύσω and συνοικήσω may be read as futures or as deliberative aorist subjunctives; after Πῶς the deliberative sense, 'how am I to…', is the natural one. καὶ τῶν κυνῶν φυλαττόντων με is a genitive absolute with καί meaning 'even', so the clause concedes rather than merely describes. ὅπου here is not local but circumstantial, 'seeing that'. Chambry sets a space before the Greek question mark.

sentences.t: Ὅτι οὐ δεῖ τινα ἀσφαλείας τῆς ἑαυτοῦ γυμνωθῆναι, τοῖς ἀκαταλλάκτοις ἐχθροῖς δι’ ὅρκων πεισθέντα.
sentences.tr: Hoti ou dei tina asphaleias tēs heautou gymnōthēnai, tois akatallaktois echthrois di’ horkōn peisthenta.
sentences.l: That one must not be stripped of one's own safety, having been won over by implacable enemies through oaths.
sentences.i: The story shows that one must not be stripped of one's own safety, won over by oaths from enemies who will never be reconciled.
sentences.n: A bare Ὅτι moral: the introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek and is supplied in the idiomatic line. γυμνόω is to strip naked, and takes the genitive of what one is stripped of — here ἀσφάλεια, the safety that the dogs themselves were. ἀκατάλλακτος is one with whom no reconciliation can be made, so no oath of his is worth anything.
